extracted.intended_audience: university educators, academics, and policymakers debating curriculum and the place of theology
extracted.subtask_description: Argument and criteria for whether Theology (religious doctrine) should be included among university sciences; examines epistemic status of religious truth, the mistaken reduction of religion to sentiment, and the relations between sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious doctrine is knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious doctrine is knowledge, 'in as full a sense as Newton’s doctrine is knowledge.' Theology should be treated as a science on the same footing as natural sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman repeatedly asserts the parity: 'religious doctrine is knowledge... University Teaching without Theology is simply unphilosophical.' Use this parity to argue for Theology's inclusion in University curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrinal facts have multiple legitimate origins
rubrics_metrics.description: The being of God and religious truths are reported by testimony, handed down by history, inferred by inductive process, brought home by metaphysical necessity, and urged by conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because religious claims rest on testimonial, historical, inductive, metaphysical, and conscience-based warrant—modes of evidence also used elsewhere—they satisfy epistemic standards used to include other subjects in a university.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of inclusion criteria across sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot consistently define University Knowledge by any single mode (senses, intuition, testimony, abstract reasoning) in a way that includes some sciences and excludes Religion without arbitrary mutilation of the circle of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you accept multiple modes of evidence for secular sciences, you must apply the same boundary logic to religion; beware exclusionary definitions that rely on a single epistemic criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious doctrines can be historical and metaphysical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines such as the Incarnation, angels, the Last Things, divine influence on the will, if true, are as much historical or metaphysical facts as any natural-historical assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat specific religious claims as you would other claims with historical or metaphysical character when judging their place in academic inquiry; their mixed character argues for academic treatment rather than exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting Theology because religion is 'sentiment' is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that Religion consists in feeling or sentiment (not in intellectual assent to revealed doctrine) is used to exclude it from knowledge; Newman argues this is a category mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about religion's epistemic status carefully: if Religion is presented merely as sentiment, it is disqualified from academic study improperly; distinguish sentimental religion from doctrinal/revealed claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith is an intellectual act with objective content
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith should be understood as an intellectual act whose object is truth and whose result is knowledge (the old Catholic notion, opposed to the purely sentimental view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding curricular inclusion, ask whether the religious instruction in question asserts definite credenda (doctrines) and thereby claims objective truth amenable to academic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'God' determines whether Theology is a science
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'God' is only a vague principle, a function of nature, or a poetic sentiment, Theology collapses into natural science; but if God is conceived as an individual, self-dependent, all-perfect Being, Theology has a distinct subject-matter and claims that warrant scientific treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess opponents' use of 'God' — if their conception is thin/deistic, their argument against Theology's distinctness is unconvincing; require precise content before conceding that Theology is reducible to other sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology addresses facts and relations like other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is 'facts and their relations'; sciences are partial abstractions that apprehend portions of the whole system of facts—Theology apprehends facts/relations concerning the Creator and so fits this definition of a science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the general definition of knowledge (facts and relations) to judge whether Theology belongs among the sciences: if it apprehends facts/relations, it conforms to the university ideal of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of sciences argues for including Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences are partial and sometimes need 'external assistance' from other sciences; because all parts of knowledge interconnect, Theology can assist and be assisted by other branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the mutual bearing between Theology and secular disciplines when designing curricula: exclusion may be prejudicial to other branches; inclusion fosters intellectual completion and mutual illumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities cannot claim to teach 'de omni scibili' while excluding religious facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A university professing to teach all knowable things cannot consistently ignore religious facts if they are believed to be true by thoughtful minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an institution claims comprehensive knowledge, enforce internal consistency by including subjects whose truth-claims fall within the institution’s declared remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware rhetorical/equivocal usages that mask substantive disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: When proponents say 'human science leads to belief in a Supreme Being' one must ask whether they mean the same substantive conception of God as religious believers; equivocal use of terms undermines the claim that Theology is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand precise definitions and substantive content in debates about curricular exclusion; do not accept superficial concessions (e.g., 'some belief in God') as defeating Theology's claim to a distinct science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying religious education as moral/sentimental instruction misplaces its aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports that place religious education under 'sentiment' (alongside poetry and music) treat it as cultivation of feelings rather than as an instruction in objective truth, thus improperly marginalizing it from serious academic study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between moral/sentimental education and doctrinal/theological instruction when determining what belongs in a university syllabus; administrative classifications that reduce religion to sentiment should be questioned.
